item.title: Pacific Islands
item.description: Tonga's Crown Prince called for Pacific countries to shift from simply building meteorological infrastructure to sustaining systems that protect realities of communities. Opening the Fourth Pacific Ministerial Meeting on Meteorology ( PMMM4 ) in Nuku'alofa on Tuesday 15 September 2026, Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala said robust weather services were no longer a luxury for Pacific countries.
item.content:encoded:
Tonga's Crown Prince called for Pacific countries to shift from simply building meteorological infrastructure to sustaining systems that protect realities of communities.

Opening the Fourth Pacific Ministerial Meeting on Meteorology ( PMMM4 ) in Nuku'alofa on Tuesday 15 September 2026, Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala said robust weather services were no longer a luxury for Pacific countries.

In his welcome address the Crown Prince said Pacific nations needed to develop their people, strengthen institutions and build the capacity required to maintain the systems on which communities depend. He emphasied that the region needs to ensure that investments in meteorological and early warning systems remained effective over the long term.

“From building systems to sustaining them,” he said. “From institutional silos to an Earth-system approach. From duplication towards greater efficiency. From fossil-fuel dependence towards resilient green services. And from weather information towards early action that protects lives and livelihoods.”

The Crown Prince said Pacific institutions did not need to become one institution, but their science, information and warning systems needed to work together. For Small Island Developing States with limited resources, he said, integration was both scientifically necessary and economically sensible.

He warned that infrastructure could become ineffective without long-term maintenance, skilled personnel and sustainable financing. A weather station that could not be maintained would eventually stop observing, while a radar that could not be repaired would eventually stop providing protection, he said.

“No warning system in our Pacific should fail because we could afford to install it but could not afford to maintain it.”

The Crown Prince also called for greater efficiency in the use of renewable energy, including reducing unnecessary duplication, sharing specialised capabilities and strengthening regional cooperation.

Renewable energy, battery storage and energy-efficient technologies could improve resilience and energy security while lowering long-term operating costs, he said.

“Our ambition should therefore be clear: Pacific meteorological services that are increasingly efficient, resilient and green.”

He said Pacific meteorological services also needed to reduce their dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The Crown Prince said meteorological services now played a role far beyond weather forecasting, supporting aviation, shipping, agriculture, fisheries, water security and tourism. They also helped protect infrastructure and communities and supported disaster preparedness, anticipatory action and disaster risk financing.

“They are therefore part of the security infrastructure of our nations. Investment in meteorology is an investment in human security, economic security and national resilience.”

He said the value of investment should ultimately be measured not by how much information was produced, but whether information reached people in time to act.

The region's goal should be to leave future generations not only more infrastructure, but stronger institutions, skilled Pacific people and sustainable systems.

The Crown Prince then formally declared PMMM4 open with deliberations to be held at Anastasis Hall in Tokomololo today.

The meeting is being held under the theme “Weather Ready for a Secured and Sustainable Blue Pacific”, bringing together Pacific ministers, meteorological officials, regional organisations and development partners to discuss the future of weather, climate and early warning services in the region.

Also attending in support of the Pacific Ministers and leaders were the President for the World Meteorological Organization ( WMO ) Abdulla Al Mandous;, the current chair of the PMMM3 Minister for Meteorology of Fiji Hon. Ro Filipe Tuisawau; and the Director General for SPRERP Sefanaia Nawadra.

item.title: Tala win over Cook Islands in Netball Cup Sydney 2027 opener
item.description: Tonga’s Tala have opened their Sydney 2027 Netball World Cup qualifying campaign with an 81-55 win over the Cook Islands at Tonga High School Indoor Stadium in Nuku’alofa. The Tala held their composure through a competitive opening quarter from Cook Islands before gradually establishing control of the match yesterday, Monday, 14 September 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Tonga’s Tala have opened their Sydney 2027 Netball World Cup qualifying campaign with an 81-55 win over the Cook Islands at Tonga High School Indoor Stadium in Nuku’alofa.

The Tala held their composure through a competitive opening quarter from Cook Islands before gradually establishing control of the match yesterday, Monday, 14 September 2026.

Tala's Goal Attacker Marie Payn maintained Tonga's advantage, while wing attacker Luana Aukafolau and centre Hulita Veve with the nation's goal shooter Uneeq Palavi produced a strong scoring performance, converting repeatedly keeping the Tala ahead.

Sixteen-year-old Ma'ume'a Jariah Kivalu also made her debut at international level, with fans and organisers praising the teenager’s skills and composure in her first match of this level.

Queen Nanasipau’u and members of the Royal Family attended in suppot of the Tongan Tala.

The fixture was the second of the day with Samoa defeating Papua New Guinea in the opening match.

Tonga will continue its qualifying campaign against Papua New Guinea later today, Tuesday, at 6:00pm, Tonga High School Indoor Stadium.

The Tala will then face Samoa in their final match of the tournament on Friday, September 18, at 6:00pm.

The qualifiers are being hosted in Tonga as part of the pathway to the Sydney 2027 Netball World Cup.

item.title: Pacific Met Council protecting communities from growing threat of climate change

item.content:encoded:
Protecting Pacific communities from the growing threats of climate change and natural disasters is a common purpose for hundreds of Pacific delegates gathered in Nuku’alofa, for the Eighth Pacific Meteorological Council ( PMC8 ). The last day of deliberations is being held today, 14 September 2026.

For two days last week, delegates debated policies, shared experiences, and examined technical papers but the message from the chair, Laitia Fifita, has been clear: at the centre of every agenda item are the people of the Pacific.

“The backbone and core of these discussions are the people. The main aim at every agenda is to protect lives and livelihoods from natural disasters,” Fifita said. “The people are the priorities of this regional council meeting, branching down to the technical aspects of meteorology such as staff, technology and equipment.”

The opening sessions revisited progress from past PMC meetings, assessing achievements and identifying gaps. Fifita acknowledged the diversity of national priorities shaped by differing populations, geographies, and vulnerabilities. While disagreements surfaced, he described them as a strength rather than a weakness.

“We all differ in opinions and goals, but we will always connect in wanting to protect our people, countries and ocean,” he said.

Fifita used the platform to outline seven objectives for Tonga’s meteorology sector, ranging from workforce empowerment and advanced technology to renewable energy transition and the role of media as a pillar in disaster preparedness.

He emphasised the need for tailored forecasts for vulnerable groups, integration with Tonga’s national development framework, and sustainability of donor-supported projects.

“After the project, what’s next? That is the question I wish to answer and fulfil so that Tonga progresses for the better,” he said.

Building a Multi-Hazard Early Warning System

Tonga’s progress in disaster preparedness was highlighted by 'Ofa Fa’anunu, Manager of the Weather Ready Pacific Programme under SPREP , who said that Tonga had already established a multi-hazard early warning policy, endorsed by the Tongan cabinet during his time as director of the Meteorological Services.

The policy paved the way for a technical group combining meteorological and disaster risk management expertise, with the new office built at Matatoa ready for it's opening.

“Tonga’s multi-hazard early warning system has been running for two years now,” Mr Fa’anunu said. “Hopefully one day the geological team can also involve in Tonga’s early warning systems.”

The second day of the council's meetings concluded on Friday, 11 September 2026 with a few agenda yet to be discussed, the agenda was to be deliberated early before the last day on Monday 14 August 2026.

The PMC8 deliberations underscore the Pacific’s determination to integrate science, policy, and community preparedness. With climate threats intensifying, the council’s outcomes are expected to guide regional cooperation and resilience-building for years to come.

item.content:encoded:
Tonga’s constitution guarantees the right to speak, write and print freely. But, when a prime minister can simply exclude a journalist from a press conference, who is actually protecting that right?

I am asking this as a young Tongan citizen. I grew up being told that our constitution – one of the oldest in the Pacific – already gives us this freedom, that it was settled 150 years ago and doesn’t need to be fought for again. So when I read the news and watch on television that a journalist was turned away from government press conferences, again and again, by a guard who couldn’t even say what rule allowed it, something in that story didn’t sit right with me. Not because I expected Tonga to be perfect. Because I expected better than silence when someone finally asked why.

On 4 September 2026, Tonga’s Supreme Court issued urgent interim orders against Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua, after ‘Etuate Lavulavu, chief executive of the Tonga Chronicle and 88. 1FM , was repeatedly denied entry to government press conferences. When he asked the security guard what regulation justified turning him away, the guard couldn’t answer. He later learned the instruction came directly from the Prime Minister’s Office. Other reporting describes his outlet being blocked from filming while other outlets were allowed to.

I don’t think this means our constitution has failed, exactly. Clause 7 still says what it has always said: that no law shall ever restrict our right to speak, write, and publish our opinions. Nobody stopped Lavulavu from writing what he thinks. What happened is narrower, and in some ways more worrying for someone my age watching this unfold – a government controlled who got into the room, on no visible legal basis, and it took a court order to fix it. Our constitution protects what we’re allowed to say. It never promised us the right to be let in the door to ask the question in the first place. It’s just being used now, in front of all of us.

This matters to my generation specifically. We are the ones who will inherit whichever version of this becomes normal – either a country where access to power is written down, equal, and can’t quietly disappear depending on who’s in charge that week, or one where it depends on court cases that most people will never have the money or the standing to bring. I don’t want to grow up watching “ask a hard question and get locked out” become just how things work here.

So this is what I’d ask for, plainly: published, written rules for who gets access to government press conferences and officials – rules that apply the same way to every outlet and can’t be overruled by a quiet phone call from someone’s office. Our government already says these briefings exist for transparency. Writing that down costs it nothing except the ability to pick and choose who gets to ask questions.

Whether that happens is not really my question to answer alone. It’s a question for everyone in Tonga who’s watching this and wondering whether this and wondering whether the next generation will inherit a stronger version of this freedom, or a weaker one dressed up in the same old words. I’d rather ask that out loud now than stay quiet and find out later.

Best regards, Malia So’afa (student), Hihifo

item.title: KlickEx partners with Tonga Post to expand money transfer services across Tonga

item.content:encoded:
KlickEx has officially announced a new strategic partnership with Tonga Post, enabling customers and members of the Tongan diaspora in Australia and New Zealand to send money transfers home for easy collection across the Kingdom.

Through this collaboration, Tonga Post will serve as an official Agent for KlickEx. Recipients in Tonga can now pick up their money transfers at four participating Tonga Post outlets located in: Nuku'alofa (Tongatapu), Vava'u, Ha'apai and 'Eua.

The partnership expands access across all four major island groups, ensuring families in remote regions can reliably access funds.

" Our mission at KlickEx has always been about making cross-border payments faster, safer, and more accessible for Pacific island communities," said Dennis Fuapau, Chief Commercial Officer at KlickEx.

" By partnering with Tonga Post, we are bridging the physical and digital divide—giving our Tongan customers in Australia and New Zealand complete flexibility to send money directly to loved ones, right across the island groups."

To use the service, senders simply log into their KlickEx account and select Tonga Post as the delivery option. Senders enter the recipient’s mobile phone number—supporting both Digicel Pacific in Tonga and Tongan Communication Corporation ( TCC ) mobile networks.

" Tonga Post is proud to collaborate with KlickEx to offer a convenient money transfer solution for families across the Kingdom of Tonga,” said Edwin Liava’a, CEO at Tonga Post.

" With key outlets in Nuku'alofa, Vava'u, Ha'apai, and 'Eua, our network ensures that essential support sent from loved ones abroad reaches recipients efficiently, securely, and close to home."

Jennifer Penisoni, Country Manager for KlickEx in Tonga, said: "The Tonga Post service is now live and available to all registered KlickEx users in Australia and New Zealand. For those not registered, signing up for a KlickEx account is simple; it takes just a few minutes. Those registering simply need their information ready - photo ID , address details and a selfie".

Mr Edwin Liava’a, at Tonga Post, said: "First-time collection requires a brief standard Know Your Customer ( KYC ) identity check. Recipients must present a valid photo ID (e.g. a driver's license or passport) at any of the Tonga Post branches during their initial money transfer pickup.”

For more information or to set up an account today, visit www.klickex.com or drop by your nearest Tonga Post branch.

Tonga Post is the national postal and logistics operator for the Kingdom of Tonga, providing mail, retail, financial, and logistics services across the Tongan islands.

KlickEx Pacific Limited, a part of the NomuPay Group, is a leading financial technology company dedicated to delivering accessible, secure, and reliable payment solutions across the Pacific region. The company’s flagship offerings include the prepaid KlickEx Visa Debit Card—enabling Pacific Islanders to travel with confidence and transact seamlessly worldwide—alongside cross-border digital settlements and mobile top-up services.

Since 2009, KlickEx Pacific Limited has remained committed to enhancing financial inclusion and fostering economic connectivity throughout the Asia-Pacific region.
